unit_label: Module B unit 1 (courseware unit 10): Fundamentals of Human Resource Management

facts.statement: Organisations are social systems that combine people and technology. Technology and processes can be copied by competitors but the people of an organisation cannot, so human resources are the main differentiator, and the emphasis has shifted from the quantity to the quality of human resources. People management is the most dynamic and enduring part of managing an organisation because, unlike other resources, which are passive, human resource reacts to the treatment given to it and its response is neither standard nor uniform.

In the past HR was seen as a necessary but unessential, unproductive department, mainly an administrative and welfare function with regular administrative and record-keeping work. Changing workforce demographics, technology, the generation gap in work ethics and globalisation changed this: as land was the source of wealth in the agrarian era, human capital is the primary source of wealth creation in the knowledge era, and HR is now expected to be a strategic partner and business catalyst.

The courseware quotes Schein: an organisation is the rational coordination of the activities of a number of people for the achievement of some common explicit purpose or goal, through division of labour and function and through a hierarchy of authority and responsibility. In a formal organisation goals, structure, roles and relationships are explicit and documented; in an informal one they evolve from group processes. Too much structure creates rigidity and slows decisions. Two interdependent streams of thought developed: how to organise activities most systematically, and how to understand the individual's relation to work. Robert Owen (1771-1858) held that a manager's best investment was in workers, whom he called vital machines, and that better conditions raise productivity; Charles Babbage (1792-1871) advocated division of labour and scientific principles of work.

Scientific management, pioneered by Frederick Taylor (1856-1915) with Gantt and Gilbreth and known for division of labour and time and motion studies, assumed that tasks can be broken into simple units, that people will do a given activity in return for money, and that people must do what the organisation and technology define. It ignored fatigue, boredom, relationships and group dynamics, treated people as replaceable, and contributed to the rise of labour unions and unrest. The courseware says these assumptions have little relevance in today's VUCA (volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity) environment.

The Hawthorne Studies by Elton Mayo and others at Western Electric (1924 to 1933) showed that emotions, relationships and work meaning affect performance. The human relations movement that followed replaced the "rational-economic man" with the "social man". Later researchers such as Chris Argyris, Abraham Maslow, Douglas McGregor and Frederick Herzberg argued that individuals are motivated by other than monetary factors: they want meaning in their activities, responsibility, a sense of achievement and involvement in deciding their activities. This was the beginning of the developmental approach to people management.

People management became a distinct function from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, as organisations grew after the Industrial Revolution. In India, Prof. A. K. Rice's 1952 experiment on group behaviour in Ahmedabad mills was significant. Welfare or social secretaries marked the birth of specialised human resource management; units such as the Time Office in textile mills and factories and the establishment section in banks and commercial offices did similar work; the term personnel officer was used first in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries in the 1960s. The fundamental activities are recruitment and selection, training and developing, performance appraisal, and reward and compensation; later came manpower assessment, career management, succession planning and talent management.
facts.locator: Printed p. 178, The Development of People Management Functions

facts.statement: Two traditions shaped personnel management: one from economics and accounting, hard-headed and profit-minded, and one from social work and social psychology, taking a social-welfare view. The conflict between them has lessened as organisations accept two primary goals, productivity and maintenance, both essential. Organisations cannot ignore employee satisfaction and wellness for their sustainability and growth.

The evolution of approaches to people management has been by addition of dimensions, not substitution. Quoting Sheth (1992), HRM assumes that managing people is an integral part of resource management in an enterprise; human beings develop a stake in it, so their motivation, development and growth are critical to the organisation, and a managerial responsibility is to harmonise the interest and growth of the organisation with those of employees at all levels, with human sensitivity, trust in people and participative management. HRM is an umbrella for all people management functions, and every manager implements a component of it, so it is a line and staff function. The function's name changed from Labour and Welfare to Personnel to HR. Sub-modules are classified as Acquisition, Development, Motivation and Maintenance (De'Cenzo, 1988); as Planning and Administration, HRD, Job and Salary, and Workers Affairs (Pareek and Rao, 1981); and as administrative, developmental and preventive (Mankidy, 1998). Conventional functions (acquisition, promotion, administration, salary and long-term benefits, grievance and discipline) are administration and maintenance; induction, development and growth, appraisal and counselling, and career planning are HRD.

Human resource development (HRD) covers procuring the right people with the right skills and attitudes and developing them for present and future needs; it is sometimes considered the most significant subsystem of HRM, and development of professionals should be continuous (continuous professional development). The structure and functions of HRM and HRD do not conflict; the difference is in approach and emphasis. Routine functions become part of HRM, while HRD emphasises organisational interventions for climate development, employee and organisational development linked with organisational goals, and change management, with the emphasis on enhancing human capital for present and future needs; it may involve surveys, research and formulation of people policies.

The role of those handling people management changed from administering attendance, output, quality, working conditions, safety and hygiene (done by supervisors) to a specialist function, because employment-related legislation required special knowledge. In banks the unions became power centres in the 1960s and 1970s and industrial relations functions emerged to deal with unions and with misconduct and disciplinary enquiries. Maturing from personnel to HRM and HRD showed that the function cannot be delinked from line managers, who are the delivery points of people management including development. There is a debate whether the function should be a specialist function or whether line managers with the right orientation can be HR functionaries; the ultimate success is decided by human relation orientation, the HR philosophy, which is not the property of any profession.

Pareek and Rao group the functions in the developmental perspective into five roles: the supportive role (strengthening the operating and executive levels), the role of systems development and research (systems dealing with people, their problems and organisational dynamics), the managerial role (planning future manpower, recruiting, placement, retaining, motivating and integrating people, performance and potential assessment, planning growth), the role of developing competence (technical, managerial and processing competence, and coping competence) and the process role (creating the culture and values needed to respond to a changing environment, diagnosing problems at organisational level and taking corrective steps).

Pareek and Rao list critical attributes of HR professionals under technical (for example knowledge of appraisal systems, tests, behavioural sciences, career planning, counselling and behavioural research), managerial (organising ability and systems development skills) and personality headings (initiative, faith in human beings, positive attitude, imagination, concern for excellence and for people, sociability, research attitude, interest in learning, ability to work as a team member); personality characteristics such as initiative, faith in human beings, concern for development of employees and ability to work as a team member are crucial. In banks HR functions are generally not performed professionally and any member of the cadre may head HR. The CII HR Competency Model lists 19 interlinked competencies for HR heads: nine behavioural (communication, initiative, drive, creativity, self-confidence, teamwork, influence, problem solving, inter-personal skills) and ten functional (business knowledge, change management, diversity management, service orientation, execution excellence, financial perspective, building expertise, personal credibility, relationship management, strategic thinking and alignment). The SHRM Competency Model lists nine: Leadership and Navigation, Ethical Practice, Business Acumen, Relationship Management, Consultation, Critical Evaluation, Global and Cultural Effectiveness, Communication and HR expertise.

An HR professional can improve by acquiring qualifications relevant to the role, holding study circle meetings, exchanging ideas with peers from other companies, interacting regularly with technical experts, and doing problem-based project studies. Qualities of a successful HR professional include leadership, freedom from bias (honesty, integrity, fearlessness, a sense of justice), understanding of human psychology, communication, counselling and problem-solving skills, passion for anonymity (passing on credit and owning up to failures) and a high level of intelligence and knowledge. Because values and beliefs are critical and are not the prerogative of any discipline, and because the future HR manager is a partner in strategic planning, a line manager with the right attitude could acquire the knowledge; the aim should be to place an individual with the required attributes, keeping both options open.

Strategic HRM is the process by which an organisation uses the knowledge, skills and abilities of its employees in formulating and executing its business strategy; more widely it links HRM with the strategic role and objectives of the organisation to improve business performance, develop organisational culture and foster innovation and flexibility, and it is proactive. Employees who are partners in formulating strategy show more commitment to its implementation. The courseware's chart sets out three HR roles: the core people role (selection, orientation, career development, motivation, compensation, welfare services, retention and termination), the organisational value-add role (HR technology services, a learning work environment, organisational development and consulting) and the business transformation role (a flexible work culture, aligning HR initiatives with business strategies, implementing change and transition, and assessing return on investment in human capital). Ulrich (1998) gave HR four mandates: partner with senior and line managers in strategy execution, be an expert in the way work is organised and executed (administrative efficiency), be a champion for employees, and be an agent of continuous transformation. In most organisations HR was still mainly a policy police and regulatory watchdog; in some banks the role is called HR Relationship Manager. A competency gap is the difference between what existing systems can do and what operations require, and HR identifies and helps close it.

Under strategic HRM in banks, HR professionals move from being the conscience of the bank, reactive and proactive, to strategic business partners and enablers. Day-to-day employee issues should be delegated to line managers, who act as local HR administrators, while HR professionals act as a centre of excellence and concentrate on core HR policies of general applicability; HR professionals should be the last, but not the first, point of contact for employee-specific issues. They need knowledge of the business, of business process re-engineering, of return on investment in human capital, and of information technology; relevant professional education (for example a Master of Human Resource Management) and continuous learning through seminars and training are needed, with a primary focus on internal customers (employees) and also on delivering value to the external customer.

In India, labour welfare officers appointed under the Factories Act initially handled recruitment of workers, muster rolls and leave records, canteens and discipline; from the early 1950s the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 added legalistic duties such as charge sheets, domestic enquiries and conciliation proceedings. By the 1960s there was demand for personnel professionals with specific knowledge, although there were no academic requirements. The Indian Institute of Personnel Management (IIPM, established 1947) and the National Institute of Labour Management (NILM) were formed in the early phase and in 1982 merged into the National Institute of Personnel Management (NIPM). J. N. Tata's emphasis on human factors and TISCO's proactive practices are cited as early examples. Employment-related laws cited include Article 16(1) of the Constitution (equal opportunity), the Employment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification of Vacancies) Act 1959, the Apprentices Act 1961, the Child Labour Act 1986, the Bonded Labour System Act 1976 and the Interstate Migrant Workmen Act 1979. The HRD approach came in the 1980s, pioneered by Udai Pareek and T V Rao; State Bank of India, State Bank of Patiala, Bank of Baroda and Canara Bank are named as banks that began HRD processes then; the National HRD Network was established in 1985 and the Indian Society for Training and Development in 1970. Recent changes include diversity, gender parity, mentorship, AI-powered recruitment and talent tools, HR analytics and employer branding.

payload.title: Why people are different from every other resource
payload.core_explanation_md:
Banks buy the same software, rent similar premises and follow the same regulations. What they cannot copy from each other is their **people**. That is why human resources are the main differentiator of an organisation, and why organisations now care more about the **quality** of their people than the number.

What makes people management different from managing money or machines?

| Other resources | People |
| --- | --- |
| Passive: do not react to how they are treated | **React**: responses are neither standard nor uniform |
| Systems and infrastructure settle down | People management stays **dynamic** and never fully stabilises |
| Can be copied by competitors | Individual skills, knowledge and attitudes cannot be copied |

Even the best strategy fails if the people who must carry it out are not convinced. Changing habits and mindset is slow, which is why implementation is harder than design.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: An organisation is first a **social system**: it combines people and technology. That is why human behaviour at work is a major subject of HR study.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two reasons people management is harder than managing physical resources.
self_check.expected_takeaway: People react to treatment and respond differently from one another, and people management never settles into a fixed system; physical resources are passive and can be standardised.

payload.title: From administrative department to strategic partner
payload.core_explanation_md:
HR has changed its place in the organisation.

| | Old perspective | Present perspective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standing | Necessary but unessential, even unproductive | Strategic partner and business catalyst |
| Work | Administration, welfare and record keeping | Talent, culture, capability and change |
| Source of wealth | Land and capital (earlier eras) | **Human capital** in the knowledge era |

What changed? Shifting workforce demographics, rapid technological change, a generation gap in work ethics and the globalisation of the economy altered how businesses operate, so people management had to change too.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Every era has a primary source of wealth: land in the agrarian era, and in the knowledge era the people who use technology: their skills, knowledge and attitudes make the difference.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the primary source of wealth creation in the knowledge era, according to the courseware?

payload.title: What an organisation is, and the two streams of thought
payload.core_explanation_md:
An **organisation** (in the courseware's quotation of Schein) is the rational coordination of the activities of many people to achieve a common, explicit purpose, through **division of labour and function** and a **hierarchy of authority and responsibility**.

- **Formal** organisation: goals, structure, roles and relationships are explicit and documented, to keep decisions consistent.
- **Informal** organisation: roles and relationships evolve from group processes.

Too much structure causes rigidity and slows decisions.

Two streams of thinking developed side by side:

1. how to **organise the activities** most systematically (the work);
2. how to understand the **individual's relation to work** (the person).

Early figures: **Robert Owen** (workers are "vital machines", so better conditions raise productivity) and **Charles Babbage** (division of labour, scientific principles of work).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The history of people management is the history of management thought: each theory of how to manage work carried an assumption about people.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two interdependent streams does the courseware identify?
self_check.expected_takeaway: How to organise activities systematically, and how to understand the individual's relation to work.

payload.title: Scientific management and why it fell short
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Frederick Taylor** (with Gantt and Gilbreth) built **scientific management** on division of labour and time-and-motion studies. Its three working assumptions:

1. Tasks can be broken into simple units that people can understand and perform.
2. People will do a given activity **in return for money**.
3. People must do what the organisation and its technology define.

**What it overlooked:** fatigue, boredom, the need to talk to colleagues, group dynamics and relationships. It treated people as replaceable, which helped fuel **labour unions** and unrest. It has little relevance today in a **VUCA** world (volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The approach was productive for simple repetitive work, but it controlled only the activities strictly related to the work and let go of everything else people bring to it.

self_check.prompt_text: Which assumption of scientific management is most clearly contradicted by later motivation research?
self_check.expected_takeaway: That people work only for money; later researchers showed meaning, responsibility and achievement also motivate.

payload.title: Hawthorne, human relations and the social man
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **Hawthorne Studies** (Elton Mayo and colleagues, Western Electric, 1924-33) found that emotions, relationships and the meaning of work affect performance. The **human relations movement** that followed swapped the **rational-economic man** (works for pay, responds to logic of work design) for the **social man** (needs belonging, recognition and good relationships).

Later researchers (Argyris, Maslow, McGregor, Herzberg) pushed further: people are motivated by **more than money**. They want to find meaning in what they do, to carry responsibility and to feel a sense of achievement. If those are missing, performance suffers.

So people management had to provide those ingredients, and this started the **developmental approach**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This also explains why people management systems began to care for relationships with supervisors, colleagues and groups.

self_check.prompt_text: What replaced the "rational-economic man" in the human relations movement?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The "social man", motivated by relationships and meaning as well as pay.

payload.title: How people management became a function
payload.core_explanation_md:
As organisations grew after the Industrial Revolution, specialised **departments** for finance, accounting and production appeared, and later one for **people**.

- Early forms: welfare or **social secretaries** to meet workers' needs and prevent unions; the **Time Office** in textile mills and factories; the **establishment section** in banks and commercial offices.
- The title **personnel officer** appeared in the 1960s (chemical and pharmaceutical industries).
- In India, Prof. A. K. Rice's 1952 group-behaviour experiment at Ahmedabad mills was a landmark.

**Core activities**: recruitment and selection; training and developing; performance appraisal; reward and compensation. **Added later**: manpower assessment, career management, succession planning, talent management.

Two traditions pulled in different directions, the **profit-minded** economics tradition and the **welfare** social-psychology tradition, until organisations accepted two goals: **productivity** and **maintenance** (employee satisfaction and wellness).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Policies that maximise one goal can damage the other, so organisations that ignore employee wellness harm their own sustainability.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four fundamental activities of people management and two of the later additions.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Recruitment and selection, training and developing, performance appraisal, reward and compensation; later manpower assessment, career management, succession planning, talent management (any two).

payload.title: HRM, personnel management and HRD
payload.core_explanation_md:
The function evolved by **adding** dimensions, never by throwing the old ones away. Its name changed from **Labour and Welfare** to **Personnel** to **HR**.

**HRM** is the **umbrella** for all people-related functions and a **line-and-staff** responsibility: every manager carries out part of it. In Sheth's words, as the courseware quotes him, it treats people as stakeholders whose development and growth are critical, seeks to harmonise their interests with the organisation's, and rests on human sensitivity, trust and participative management.

**How the functions are classified:**

| Classification | Groups |
| --- | --- |
| De'Cenzo | Acquisition, Development, Motivation, Maintenance |
| Pareek and Rao | Planning and Administration, HRD, Job and Salary, Workers Affairs |
| Mankidy | Administrative, Developmental, Preventive |

**Administration and maintenance**: acquisition, promotion, administration, salary and long-term benefits, grievance and discipline. **HRD**: induction, development and growth, appraisal and counselling, career planning.

**HRM and HRD**: no conflict in structure or functions; the difference is **approach and emphasis**. HRM covers routine people functions; HRD emphasises organisation-wide interventions (climate, employee and organisational development tied to goals, change management) and building human capital. HRD is sometimes treated as the most significant subsystem of HRM.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Exam answers often hinge on this point: HRM and HRD are related, HRD sits within the HRM umbrella, and their difference lies in emphasis, not in separate departments.

self_check.prompt_text: Is succession planning an administrative or a developmental function?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Developmental (HRD): it identifies and prepares people to replace key functionaries.

payload.title: The role of HR professionals: five roles and the line manager
payload.core_explanation_md:
As the function matured from personnel to HRM and HRD, its professionals moved from policing attendance and discipline to developing people and systems.

**Pareek and Rao's five roles** (as the courseware reports them):

| Role | Focus |
| --- | --- |
| **Supportive** | Strengthen operating and executive levels |
| **Systems development and research** | Systems that deal with people, their problems and organisational dynamics |
| **Managerial** | Plan manpower, recruit, place, retain, motivate, appraise, plan growth |
| **Developing competence** | Technical, managerial and processing competence; coping competence |
| **Process** | Culture and values, diagnosing organisation-level problems, corrective steps |

**Line managers** are the **delivery points** for people management, including development, so HR cannot be delinked from them. Whether HR heads must be trained specialists or can be line managers with the right outlook is an open debate; what decides success is the HR philosophy (values), which is not the property of any one profession.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Statutory obligations and strong unions made HR a specialist function in banks during the 1960s to 1980s: industrial relations and disciplinary enquiries needed legal knowledge.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of the five roles concerns culture, values and corrective steps at organisation level?

payload.title: What makes an effective HR professional: attributes and competency models
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Attributes** (Pareek and Rao): technical (appraisal systems, tests, behavioural sciences, career planning, counselling, behavioural research); managerial (organising ability, systems development skills); and **personality** (initiative, faith in human beings, positive attitude, concern for excellence and for people, teamwork, interest in learning). The personality group matters most: without initiative, faith in people, concern for employees' development and teamwork, the technical knowledge achieves little.

**Competency models:**

| Model | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **CII HR Competency Model** | **19** competencies for HR heads: **9 behavioural** (communication, initiative, drive, creativity, self-confidence, teamwork, influence, problem solving, inter-personal skills) and **10 functional** (business knowledge, change management, diversity management, service orientation, execution excellence, financial perspective, building expertise, personal credibility, relationship management, strategic thinking and alignment) |
| **SHRM Competency Model** | **9**: Leadership and Navigation, Ethical Practice, Business Acumen, Relationship Management, Consultation, Critical Evaluation, Global and Cultural Effectiveness, Communication, HR expertise |

In banks, HR is generally a generalist cadre posting rather than a professional specialisation.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A successful HR professional is expected to be free from bias (honest, fearless, with a sense of justice), skilled in human relations and counselling, and willing to pass on credit and own up to failures.

self_check.prompt_text: How many competencies are in the CII HR Competency Model, and how do they divide?

payload.title: Strategic HRM: linking people to business strategy
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Strategic HRM** is the process of using employees' knowledge, skills and abilities in **formulating and carrying out** the business strategy. More broadly it links HRM with the organisation's strategic objectives to improve business performance, build culture and foster innovation and flexibility. It is **proactive**, and employees who help form strategy are more committed to it.

**Three HR roles** (courseware chart):

| Role | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Core people** | Selection, orientation, career development, motivation, compensation, welfare, retention and termination |
| **Organisational value-add** | HR technology services, a learning work environment, organisational development and consulting |
| **Business transformation** | A flexible work culture, aligning HR with business strategy, implementing change, measuring return on investment in human capital |

**Ulrich's four mandates:** partner with senior and line managers in strategy execution; expert in how work is organised (administrative efficiency); champion for employees; agent of continuous transformation.

A **competency gap** is the difference between what the present systems can do and what operations require; strategic HR identifies it and closes it.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Compare with the old picture of HR as "policy police" and regulatory watchdog handling paperwork on hiring and firing.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two of Ulrich's four mandates.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: partner in strategy execution; expert in organising work efficiently; champion for employees; agent of continuous transformation.

payload.title: New roles for HR professionals in banks
payload.core_explanation_md:
Under strategic HRM, a bank's HR professionals move from being the bank's **conscience** (reactive, and proactive when needed) to **strategic business partners and enablers**.

- **Delegate day-to-day employee issues to line managers**, who act as local HR administrators.
- HR professionals become a **centre of excellence**, concentrating on **core policies** of general application.
- HR should be the **last, not the first**, point of contact on an employee-specific issue.
- They need **business knowledge**, understanding of **business process re-engineering** and **return on investment in human capital**, and **information technology** skills.
- Education: relevant professional programmes (such as a Master of Human Resource Management) and continuous learning through seminars and training.
- Focus on **internal customers** (employees) and on delivering value to the **external customer** too.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The old model, where only HR handled employee issues and line managers just extracted work, is described as out-lived.

self_check.prompt_text: In the new model, who is the first point of contact for an employee-specific issue?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The line manager; HR is the last, not the first, point of contact.

India followed a path similar to the West, shaped by British rule and the world wars.

| Independence era | **Labour welfare officers** under the **Factories Act**: recruiting, muster rolls and leave records, canteens, discipline |
| From the 1950s | **Industrial Disputes Act 1947** added legalistic duties: charge sheets, domestic enquiries, conciliation proceedings |

options.explanation_md: The courseware says the function cannot be delinked, not abolished.

options.text_md: They are the delivery points of people management, including development
options.explanation_md: The HR function cannot be delinked from line managers.

options.text_md: They have no role in HR

payload.correct_explanation_md: Line managers are the delivery points of people management.

payload.stem_md: Which of Pareek and Rao's five roles concerns creating the culture and values the organisation needs to respond to its changing environment?

options.explanation_md: This strengthens operating and executive levels.
This covers manpower planning, recruitment, appraisal and so on.
It covers culture and values, diagnosing problems and corrective steps.
This concerns developing systems dealing with people.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The process role covers creating culture and values and taking corrective steps at organisational level.

payload.stem_md: The CII HR Competency Model for HR heads lists 19 interlinked competencies. How are they divided?

options.explanation_md: This is the division in the courseware.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The model has nine behavioural and ten functional competencies.

payload.stem_md: On whether HR functionaries should be specialists or line managers, the courseware concludes that

options.text_md: The aim should be to place an individual with the required attributes and values, keeping both options open
options.explanation_md: Values are not the prerogative of any discipline.

options.text_md: Only HR graduates can be HR functionaries
options.explanation_md: The courseware keeps both options open.

options.text_md: Only line managers should be HR functionaries
HR needs no knowledge of the business
options.explanation_md: HR needs business knowledge for strategic planning.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The courseware favours placing someone with the required attributes, whether specialist or line manager.

payload.stem_md: Strategic HRM is best described as

options.text_md: Keeping personnel records up to date
Linking HR strategy and practices with the business strategy and objectives to improve business performance

payload.correct_explanation_md: Strategic HRM integrates HR with the strategic role and objectives of the organisation.

payload.stem_md: Which of Ulrich's four mandates involves representing employees' concerns to senior management while raising their contribution?

options.explanation_md: This is about working with senior and line managers.

options.text_md: Expert in how work is organised

options.explanation_md: The champion represents employees' concerns and increases their commitment and contribution.
This is about shaping processes and culture for change.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The "champion for employees" role represents employee concerns and increases employee contribution.

payload.stem_md: A competency gap is

options.text_md: The difference between two employees' salaries
The time between recruitment and promotion
A gap in the HR budget
The difference between what existing systems can do and what operational requirements demand
options.explanation_md: HR identifies and helps close such gaps.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A competency gap is the difference between the ability of existing systems and what is expected of them.

payload.stem_md: Under strategic HRM in banks, who should be the first point of contact for an employee-specific issue?

options.explanation_md: Line managers act as local HR administrators for day-to-day issues.
HR is the last, not the first, point of contact.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Day-to-day employee issues are delegated to line managers; HR is the last point of contact.

payload.stem_md: In India, labour welfare officers were initially appointed under which Act, with duties such as recruitment, records, canteens and discipline?

options.explanation_md: This provides for training linked to employment.
This is the Act named in the courseware.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Labour welfare officers were appointed under the Factories Act.

payload.stem_md: The National Institute of Personnel Management (NIPM) was formed in 1982 by the merger of

options.text_md: ISTD and the National HRD Network

payload.correct_explanation_md: The Indian Institute of Personnel Management and the National Institute of Labour Management merged to form NIPM.

payload.stem_md: The HRD approach was introduced in India in the 1980s mainly through the work of

options.text_md: J. N. Tata and A. K. Rice
options.explanation_md: They are cited for earlier contributions.

options.text_md: Udai Pareek and T V Rao
options.explanation_md: They are credited with clarifying HRD focus and developing HRD systems.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Udai Pareek and T V Rao pioneered HRD in India in the 1980s.

payload.stem_md: The courseware cites J. N. Tata and TISCO as examples of

options.text_md: Early, proactive attention to human factors in an organisation
options.explanation_md: They show what proactivity means in people management.

payload.correct_explanation_md: TISCO's proactive practices illustrate early attention to human factors.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT one of the nine competencies in the SHRM Competency Model listed in the courseware?

options.explanation_md: This is a scientific management technique, not an SHRM competency.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The SHRM model lists Leadership and Navigation, Ethical Practice, Business Acumen, Relationship Management, Consultation, Critical Evaluation, Global and Cultural Effectiveness, Communication and HR expertise.
